newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Saint's holiday pushes Brazil reform votes to July.
newsitem.headline: Saint's holiday pushes Brazil reform votes to July.

text.p: Brazilian holidays to celebrate the feast day of St John means there is no chance of the government making headyway with long-awaited votes on its civil service reform bill before July, a senior whip said.

"We can't kid ourselves, we have to work with the reality of Congress," said Deputy Aecio Neves, the lower house leader of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party (PSDB).
St John, or Sao Joao as he is known in Brazil, is revered in the country's north and northeastern where his June 24 feast day is celebrated with week-long parties, bonfires and fireworks.
Traditionally, local lawmakers are among the guests of honor at the parties and, with next year's elections looming, they are expected to stay at home en masse next week.
That will make it impossible for the government to muster the three-fifths majorities it needs to kill opposition amendments to the civil service reform bill, Neves told national CBN radio.
"We'll spend the week instead deepening negotiations (over the reform) seeing as the subject is of such great importance to the country," the lawmaker said.

He said voting on the outstanding amendments, which has already dragged on for more than two months, might resume in the first week of July, paving the way for a second and final vote on the bill in the lower house itself by the end of the month.
Congress normally is in recess in July, but the government is expected to call a month-long extraordinary session to make up for lost time on its flagging reform drive.

That would give partying lawmakers another reason to celebrate -- members of Congress are entitled to triple pay if summoned to an extraordinary session, taking their salary for the month to about $23,000.

The civil service reform, if approved in the Chamber of Deputies, would advance to the Senate. Another key reform of the pensions system is currently in the upper house, but will have to return to the chamber for approval of recent changes.
